newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Russia overshadows Kazakh debt ratings.
newsitem.headline: Russia overshadows Kazakh debt ratings.

text.p: Russia's hold over Kazakhstan's oil wealth has affected its debt ratings as Kazakhstan nears its first Eurobond issue, expected before the end of the year, Western investors said.
"With a more stable political base, some in the market felt Kazakhstan deserved a higher rating than Russia," said one western financier, based in the capital Almaty.
But topping the list of rating agency concerns were Kazakhstan's relations with its former overlord Russia.

Moody's, an international rating agency which gave Kazakhstan a Ba3 sovereign ceiling for long-term foreign currency bonds, said Russia was "pursuing a fairly blatant policy of economic imperialism towards Kazakhstan".

Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev constantly underlines the importance of good relations with Russia. He recently called for members of the Commonwealth of Independent States to reaffirm their commitment to the post-Soviet grouping.

Oil executives planning to invest billions of dollars in the country's energy sector, however, watch Kazakh-Russian relations like hawks, fearing the effect any discord might have on proposals to export crude, the future basis of Kazakh wealth, to western markets.

Kazakhstan is now almost totally reliant on Russian pipelines to export the bulk of its crude. A planned $1.5 billion pipeline will export oil from Kazakhstan's rich Tengiz oil field through Russia to the latter's Black Sea port of Novorossiisk.
"I think the same rating as Russia is appropriate -- Russia is a major trading partner and force in the region," said one banker.
Standard and Poor's and London-based IBCA both gave Kazakhstan BB- for long-term foreign currency ratings -- Russia received a Ba2 rating from Moody's, BB- from Standard and Poor's and BB+ from IBCA.
"I think the ratings are still pretty positive," said Peter Phelps of brokers Global Kazkommerts Securities. "It puts Kazakhstan on a par with Russia, Turkey and India," he said.
Kazakh officials say they plan to issue a $100 million three-year bond this month or in December, which will be lead-managed by ABN AMRO Hoare Govett.
The purpose of the issue is to put the remote, oil-rich nation of desert, mountain and steppe, on the international financial map rather than to raise funds, say officials.

"I think there are some infrastructural problems that could drag down reforms," said one western financial analyst, who spoke on condition of anonymity. "I think it was fair of the agencies to recognise those risks."

Many western investors had thought Kazakhstan's strong, stable government, its committment to tight fiscal and monetary policies and its large mineral wealth would see it grab a better rating than Russia.
"The republic's surfeit of natural resources has already attracted foreign direct investment and led to solid export earnings," said the Moody's statement on Monday.
But along with Moody's and Standard and Poor's, IBCA pointed to Russia and its hold over Kazakhstan's oil wealth as a constraint on its rating.

"Kazakhstan's potential as an oil and gas producer, with reserves nearly as large as those of Kuwait, is enormous but its landlocked position in Central Asia continues to make it reliant on Russia and other neighbours for access to western markets," IBCA said last week.
